title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.
In this analysis, I look at median home value across counties in Maryland, and ask which communities we measure most and least reliably. As someone house-hunting in the Baltimore, I wanted to know how reliable home value estimates really are before treating them as fact. This matters beyond my own search as well since, shaky estimates affect property tax assessments and lending decisions too, so it’s useful for anyone relying on this data, not just buyers.

text:

my_state <- "MD"        # two-letter abbreviation, in quotes
my_variable <- "B25077_001"     # the variable code, in quotes

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: How big is the margin of error?
text:
How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)

Now sort to see which counties are measured least reliably.

county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 4

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                          myvarE myvarM   popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                          <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
1 24001 Allegany County, Maryland     149200   5832  67762    NA
2 24003 Anne Arundel County, Maryland 450300   4485 590936    NA
3 24005 Baltimore County, Maryland    330000   3148 849586    NA
4 24009 Calvert County, Maryland      440200   8554  93791    NA
5 24011 Caroline County, Maryland     272400   7506  33406    NA
6 24013 Carroll County, Maryland      406400   7074 174318    NA



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 2  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 4 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         12        458292.
2 Low confidence           5         28596.
3 Moderate                 7         75465.


High-confidence counties average about 458,000 people. That’s roughly 16 times more than low-confidence counties (about 29,000), with moderate counties in between at about 75,000. This matches what I expected: the ACS samples fewer households in smaller counties, so their estimates carry more uncertainty. Simply put, the most populated counties have the smallest margin of error and thus the highest confidence, and vice-versa

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
The Maryland counties we know least about, statistically speaking, are Kent, Somerset, Garrett, and Dorchester. Each shows the highest moe_pct in the dataset, meaning their median home value estimates carry the largest margin of error relative to the estimate itself. This isn’t a coincidence: these are also the state’s least populated counties, and since the ACS is a sample survey, smaller counties yield smaller samples, which produces less statistically reliable estimates. Large, densely populated counties like Montgomery, Prince George’s, and Baltimore City, by contrast, are surveyed far more heavily and show much smaller margins of error.
If a state agency used median home value to allocate funding, for example, directing more support toward counties with lower home values and treated every county’s number as equally certain; the small, low-reliability counties would bear all the risk. If a county like Somerset’s true home value is actually higher than its shaky estimate suggests, it risks receiving too little funding relative to its real need. If the true value is actually lower, it risks receiving more than it needs, pulling funding away from counties that could use it more. Meanwhile, large counties like Montgomery are essentially unaffected by this risk, since their estimates are already precise. In short, the places we measure least reliably are exactly the places most likely to be misjudged when that data drives real decisions.

title: Verify the Claim: Philadelphia Poverty Change
text: This report tests whether the ACS data supports the claims in Alfred Lubrano’s 2018 article, “New Census figures on Philly neighborhoods show inequality, high numbers of whites living in poverty” (WHYY / Philadelphia Inquirer, December 6, 2018).

title: Verify the Claim: Philadelphia Poverty Change
text:
Setup


View Code
library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)
library(sf)
library(gt)
#| include: false
options(tigris_progress = FALSE)
options(tigris_use_cache = TRUE)

title: Verify the Claim: Philadelphia Poverty Change
text:
Part 1: Reconstruct

Variables
I pulled four ACS variables. For overall poverty, B17001_002 counts people below the poverty level in the past twelve months, and B17001_001 gives the population for whom poverty status is determined. Because several claims are specifically about white poverty, I also pulled B17001A_001 and B17001A_002, the same table restricted to people identifying as white alone. ACS publishes counts, not rates, so both the rate and its margin of error have to be calculated. I used the 2006-2010 and 2013-2017 five-year estimates at the census tract level. Five-year estimates are the only ones that reach tracts; one-year estimates cover only areas of 65,000 people or more.


Assumptions
The article does not document its method, so several choices are mine. It does not name the ACS table it used; I assumed B17001. It says “white” without defining it, so I used B17001A, white alone, which includes people who also identify as Hispanic. And it reports neighborhood figures, which are not Census geographies: its reporters aggregated tracts into boundaries of their own choosing and never published which tracts went where, so my numbers will not match theirs. Every figure in the article is a point estimate, with no margins of error given.


Overlap
The two periods do not overlap. Census Bureau guidance is explicit that only non-overlapping five-year estimates should be compared over time, so on this point the article is on solid ground.

title: Verify the Claim: Philadelphia Poverty Change
text:
Part 2: Test (code plus interpretation)

Computing poverty rates
ACS publishes counts, not rates, so both the rate and its uncertainty have to be built. Dividing the count below poverty by the universe gives the rate; moe_prop() then combines the two margins of error into a margin of error for the resulting proportion. The count’s margin of error does not carry over.


View Code
pov_2010 <- pov_2010 %>%
  mutate(
    pov_pct = pov_poorE / pov_totalE * 100,
    pov_moe = moe_prop(pov_poorE, pov_totalE, pov_poorM, pov_totalM) * 100,
    wht_pct = wht_poorE / wht_totalE * 100,
    wht_moe = moe_prop(wht_poorE, wht_totalE, wht_poorM, wht_totalM) * 100
    )




View Code
pov_2017 <- pov_2017 %>%
  mutate(
    pov_pct = pov_poorE / pov_totalE * 100,
    pov_moe = moe_prop(pov_poorE, pov_totalE, pov_poorM, pov_totalM) * 100,
    wht_pct = wht_poorE / wht_totalE * 100,
    wht_moe = moe_prop(wht_poorE, wht_totalE, wht_poorM, wht_totalM) * 100
    )




Assessing reliability
The coefficient of variation (CV) expresses the uncertainty as a share of the estimate, which makes estimates comparable. Following Jurjevich et al. (2018), I flagged a CV under 12% as reliable, 12 to 40% as somewhat reliable, and above 40% as unreliable.


View Code
pov_2010 <- pov_2010 %>%
  mutate(
    pov_cv = (pov_moe/1.645) / pov_pct * 100,
    pov_reliability = case_when(
    pov_cv < 12 ~ "Reliable",
    pov_cv < 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
    pov_cv >= 40 ~ "Unreliable",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  )




View Code
pov_2010 <- pov_2010 %>%
  mutate(
    wht_cv = (wht_moe/1.645) / wht_pct * 100,
    wht_reliability = case_when(
    wht_cv < 12 ~ "Reliable",
    wht_cv < 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
    wht_cv >= 40 ~ "Unreliable",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  )




View Code
pov_2017 <- pov_2017 %>%
  mutate(
    pov_cv = (pov_moe/1.645) / pov_pct * 100,
    pov_reliability = case_when(
    pov_cv < 12 ~ "Reliable",
    pov_cv < 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
    pov_cv >= 40 ~ "Unreliable",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  )




View Code
pov_2017 <- pov_2017 %>%
  mutate(
    wht_cv = (wht_moe/1.645) / wht_pct * 100,
    wht_reliability = case_when(
    wht_cv < 12 ~ "Reliable",
    wht_cv < 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
    wht_cv >= 40 ~ "Unreliable",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  )




Observations
Reliability differs sharply between the two measures, and between the two periods. For overall poverty, 45 of 384 tracts were unreliable in 2006-2010, falling to 22 by 2013-2017. For white poverty the picture is far worse: 189 tracts, just under half the city, were unreliable in 2006-2010, improving to 111 by 2013-2017. This asymmetry matters because the article’s white poverty claims are claims about change, and a change is only as sound as its weaker endpoint. In roughly half of Philadelphia, that endpoint will not hold.


Measuring change
To compare the two periods, each tract’s 2010 and 2017 rates have to sit in the same row, so I joined the two datasets on GEOID. The change itself is simple subtraction, but its uncertainty is not: a difference between two estimates is less certain than either estimate alone, and the two margins of error combine by squaring, adding, and taking the square root rather than by simple addition. Dividing the change by that combined standard error gives a z score, which says how large the movement is relative to the noise around it. At 90% confidence the threshold is 1.645: above it, the change is distinguishable from zero; below it, the data cannot establish that anything happened.


View Code
pov_change <- pov_2010 %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(GEOID, NAME, pov_pct, pov_moe, wht_pct, wht_moe) %>%
  rename(pov_pct_10 = pov_pct, pov_moe_10 = pov_moe,
         wht_pct_10 = wht_pct, wht_moe_10 = wht_moe) %>%
  left_join(
    pov_2017 %>%
      select(GEOID, pov_pct, pov_moe, wht_pct, wht_moe) %>%
      rename(pov_pct_17 = pov_pct, pov_moe_17 = pov_moe,
             wht_pct_17 = wht_pct, wht_moe_17 = wht_moe),
    by = "GEOID"
  )




View Code
pov_change <- pov_change %>%
  mutate(
    pov_change = pov_pct_17 - pov_pct_10,
    pov_se_diff = sqrt((pov_moe_10/ 1.645)^2 + (pov_moe_17/ 1.645)^2),
    pov_moe_diff = pov_se_diff * 1.645,
    pov_z = pov_change / pov_se_diff,
    pov_sig = abs(pov_z) > 1.645
    )




View Code
pov_change <- pov_change %>%
  mutate(
    wht_change = wht_pct_17 - wht_pct_10,
    wht_se_diff = sqrt((wht_moe_10/ 1.645)^2 + (wht_moe_17/ 1.645)^2),
    wht_moe_diff = wht_se_diff * 1.645,
    wht_z = wht_change / wht_se_diff,
    wht_sig = abs(wht_z) > 1.645
    )




Missing values
Eight tracts produce no poverty rate in one or both periods. Seven of them carry numbers in the 9803 to 9809 range, which the Census Bureau reserves for special land use tracts: large areas with little or no residential population, such as parks, airports, and industrial or employment zones.
The eighth, Tract 50, sits at the southern tip of the city along the Delaware and behaves the same way. In all eight, the population for whom poverty status can be determined is effectively zero, so there is no rate to compute and the NA is correct rather than a gap in the data. I excluded them from the tract counts that follow.
Six further tracts drop out of the white poverty analysis for a different reason. Each has a measurable white poverty rate in one period but not the other, because the white population for whom poverty status could be determined was zero in the other period. Tract 103 is the clearest case: a white poverty rate of 100% in 2006-2010 and no measurable white population at all by 2013-2017. With no second endpoint there is no change to test, so these tracts are excluded from the white analysis but retained in the overall one.


View Code
count(pov_change, pov_sig)


# A tibble: 2 × 2
  pov_sig     n
  <lgl>   <int>
1 FALSE     313
2 TRUE       63




How many tracts changed
Of the 376 tracts with a measurable poverty rate in both periods, 63 show a change that is statistically distinguishable from zero at 90% confidence. The remaining 313, just over 83%, do not. That does not mean poverty held steady in those tracts; it means the data cannot establish that it moved. For most of Philadelphia, the margin of error on a seven-year change is wider than the change itself.


View Code
pov_change  %>%
  arrange(pov_change) %>%
  mutate(rank = row_number()) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = rank, y = pov_change)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = pov_change - pov_moe_diff,
                    ymax = pov_change + pov_moe_diff,
                    color = pov_sig),
                    width = 0, alpha = 0.4)+
  geom_point(aes(color = pov_sig), size = 0.5)+
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("TRUE" = "#1f5c8b", "FALSE" = "grey75"),
    labels = c("TRUE" = "Detectable", "FALSE" = "Not detectable"),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 376, by = 50)) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-60, 60)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "grey30"),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 7, color = "grey50", hjust = 0),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 9, color = "grey30"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 8),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 8),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Most Philadelphia tracts show no detectable change in poverty",
    subtitle = "Poverty rate change between the 2006-2010 and 2013-2017 ACS estimates",
    caption = str_wrap("Axis limited to ±60 points for readability; a small number of tracts have margins of error exceeding the possible range of the scale.", 100),
     x = "Each tract, ordered from largest decline to largest increase", 
    y = "Change in poverty rate (% points)"
  )









The article’s most striking white poverty figures are its lowest ones: 2% in Holmesburg, 1% in Mayfair. The table below shows the fifteen Philadelphia tracts with the lowest white poverty rates in 2006-2010, the period those claims start from. Every one of them carries a coefficient of variation above the reliability threshold, several by an order of magnitude. A rate of 1% or 2% in a tract with few white residents is not a precise measurement of a small number; it is an imprecise measurement that happens to land on a small number.

title: Verify the Claim: Philadelphia Poverty Change
section: Where the article’s smallest numbers come from
text:
Where the article’s smallest numbers come from
The article’s most striking white poverty figures are its smallest: 2% in Holmesburg, 1% in Mayfair. The first table below shows the fifteen tracts with the lowest white poverty rates in 2006-2010, the period those claims start from. Thirteen of the fifteen are unreliable.


View Code
pov_2010 %>%
   filter(!is.na(wht_pct), wht_pct > 0, wht_pct < 10) %>%
  arrange(wht_pct) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15) %>%
  mutate(
    dot = case_when(
      wht_cv < 12 ~ "🟢",
      wht_cv <= 40 ~ "🟡",
      TRUE ~ "🔴"
    ),
    NAME = str_remove(NAME, ", Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania")
  ) %>%
  select(dot, NAME, wht_pct, wht_moe, wht_cv, wht_reliability) %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(columns = c(wht_pct, wht_moe, wht_cv), decimals = 1) %>%
  cols_label(
    dot = "",
    NAME = "Tract",
    wht_pct = "Rate (%)",
    wht_moe = "MOE",
    wht_cv = "CV (%)",
    wht_reliability = "Reliability"
  ) %>%
  cols_align(align = "center", columns = dot) %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "The lowest white poverty rates are the least reliable",
    subtitle = "Fifteen tracts with the lowest white poverty rates, 2006-2010 ACS"

title: Verify the Claim: Philadelphia Poverty Change
text:
Part 3 : Adjudicate
Supported: The citywide poverty rate of 26% holds: aggregating all 384 tracts gives 25.8%, margin of error half a percentage point. This is the article’s largest-scale claim and its most secure one, because summing 384 tracts shrinks the relative error to a fraction of what it is in any single tract. The article is also right not to compare overlapping periods.
Not supported: The citywide white poverty figure (14.8% to 19.4%) comes from a one-year survey dropped into a story otherwise built on five-year estimates; Census guidance says not to compare the two. The framing fails too. Of 376 tracts, 36 show a detectable increase, 27 show a detectable decline the article never mentions, and 313 show no change distinguishable from zero. That is not a city sliding into poverty. It is a city where most places held steady and the rest moved both ways.
Cannot be determined: Philadelphia neighborhoods are not Census geographies, and the reporters never published which tracts they aggregated into which neighborhood. Fairhill’s 61%, Eastwick’s 12% to 26%, Holmesburg’s 2% to 19%, Mayfair’s 1% to 14%, and the 22-neighborhood claim are therefore uncheckable. The white poverty claims fail twice over: only 6 of 384 tracts produce a reliable white poverty rate, and 189 are unreliable outright. A 1% or 2% rate in a tract with few white residents is not a precise measurement of a small number. It is an imprecise measurement that lands on one.

title: Verify the Claim: Philadelphia Poverty Change
text:
Part 4: Rewrite
Rewriting the article’s opening paragraph:

A new five-year federal survey puts Philadelphia’s poverty rate at about 26%, a figure the data supports with precision. What it does not support is a story of a city uniformly sliding into poverty. The Census divides Philadelphia into roughly 380 small statistical areas. Between the 2006-2010 and 2013-2017 surveys, fewer than 10% of them show a poverty increase large enough to be told apart from survey error. About 7% show a decrease. The remaining 83% moved too little, or were measured too imprecisely, to say either way. The survey is weakest where the headlines are loudest: in half the city it cannot measure white poverty reliably at all, because too few white residents live there to sample well. Philadelphia’s poverty is real and citywide. Whether it is rising or falling block by block is mostly beyond what this data can show.

This is not a competition. There’s no leaderboard and no target RMSE. The goal is to practice the full prediction workflow on a question you choose, and to find out what actually helps. Some features you’re sure will help won’t, and some you add on a whim will. Both are findings.

Part 0: Setup

[1] TRUE



The cross-validation helper
This function runs 10-fold cross-validation with the same seed every time, so every model in your log is tested on the same folds. You don’t need to change it. Read it once so you know what it does.


Code
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1: don't drop rows).")
  }
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)
  fit$results$RMSE
}




The model log
Every time you fit a new model, add a row. By the end, this table is the story of your assignment.

Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal
Many of the city’s datasets on OpenDataPhilly are served through a Carto SQL API. You send a SQL query in a URL, and it sends back data. Ask for format=GeoJSON and st_read() reads the result directly, just like the Indego feed in Week 4.
The pattern:
https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=SELECT ... FROM table_name WHERE ...
Three pieces of SQL are all you need:

SELECT the_geom, column1, column2 chooses which columns come back. Always include the_geom, or you get no geometry.
FROM table_name chooses the dataset.
WHERE ... filters rows. Filter in the query, not in R. Some tables have millions of rows, and pulling everything will be slow or fail.

This helper builds the URL for you. Spaces and symbols in a URL need encoding, and URLencode() handles that.


Code
carto_get <- function(sql) {
  url <- paste0("https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=", URLencode(sql))
  st_read(url, quiet = TRUE)
}



Finding a table name
On a dataset’s OpenDataPhilly page, look for the API link. The table name is the word after FROM in the example query. To see what values a column takes before you filter on it, ask for a count in CSV format:


Code
# What kinds of crime are in the incidents table in 2023?
url <- paste0("https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=csv&q=",
              URLencode("SELECT text_general_code, COUNT(*) AS n
                         FROM incidents_part1_part2
                         WHERE dispatch_date >= '2023-01-01' AND dispatch_date < '2024-01-01'
                         GROUP BY text_general_code ORDER BY n DESC"))
read_csv(url)

Part 4: Building spatial features
Every feature below reuses a Week 4 tool. The worked examples use burglaries and Indego stations; you build the same types from your own layers.

4A: Counting
How many burglaries fall in each tract?


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(n_burglary = lengths(st_intersects(., burglary)))

summary(tracts$n_burglary)


   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  0.000   4.000   7.000   9.458  13.000  48.000 


A tract with no burglaries gets 0, not NA, so Rule 1 is safe.


4B: Density: don’t skip this
Raw counts mostly measure tract size. A big tract has more of everything. Normalize by area, by population, or by housing units, depending on what makes sense for the thing you’re counting.


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    area_sqmi         = as.numeric(st_area(.)) / 27878400,   # sq ft in a sq mile
    burglary_per_sqmi = n_burglary / area_sqmi,
    burglary_per_1k   = n_burglary / total_popE * 1000
  )








NotePer capita in low-population tracts



If a tract has 40 residents and 3 burglaries, its rate is 75 per 1,000, which is a huge number built on tiny counts. Look at the tracts with the highest per-capita rates before you trust them. This is the Week 3 lesson about small denominators again.




4C: Measuring distance to the nearest thing
How far is each tract from its nearest Indego station? Use the Week 4 pattern: find the nearest feature, then measure to it element by element.


Code
stations <- st_read("https://www.rideindego.com/stations/json/", quiet = TRUE) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

tract_pts <- st_point_on_surface(tracts)   # always inside the tract, unlike a centroid

nearest_idx <- st_nearest_feature(tract_pts, stations)

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_station_mi = as.numeric(
    st_distance(tract_pts, stations[nearest_idx, ], by_element = TRUE)) / 5280)




4D: Measuring distance to one place
Sometimes the “thing” is a single location, such as City Hall as a stand-in for the center of the regional economy.


Code
city_hall <- st_sfc(st_point(c(-75.1636, 39.9526)), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_ch_mi = as.numeric(st_distance(tract_pts, city_hall)) / 5280)

title: Assignment: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 5: Transforming features
Watch the October 9 recorded lecture before you start this part. Below is a summary to work from.
So far, every predictor has entered the model as a straight line: each additional unit of X changes predicted Y by the same amount, everywhere. Transformations let the model bend. For prediction, the question is simply does the bend lower CV RMSE? For interpretation, each transformation changes what a coefficient means, so you need to know how to read it.






TipTransform predictors, not your outcome



Keep your outcome y untransformed in this assignment. If you model log(y), your CV RMSE comes out in log units and can’t be compared to the other rows in your log. (Predicting a logged outcome well requires back-transforming, which is an A4 topic.)



5A: Logs, for skewed predictors
Many urban variables are skewed: a few tracts have huge values, and most have small ones. Income, density, and counts are typical. A log compresses the long tail, so a model can use the difference between 1 and 10 as well as the difference between 100 and 1,000.


Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = jobs_per_sqmi)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()









Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = log1p(jobs_per_sqmi))) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()











Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = pop_per_sqmi)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()









Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = log1p(pop_per_sqmi))) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()















Warninglog(0) doesn’t exist



log(0) is -Inf, and it will break your model. Counts and densities often include zeros. Use log1p(x), which computes log(x + 1), for anything that can be 0.


Reading the coefficient: when a predictor is logged, a 1% increase in X goes with a change of about β/100 in Y, in Y’s units. With log1p, this reading is approximate for small values of X.


5B: Squared terms, for curves
If your scatterplot bends (rising and then flattening, or falling and then rising), a squared term lets the line curve. Write it with I(), which tells R to do the arithmetic rather than read ^ as formula syntax.


Code
m_sq <- lm(y ~ dist_ch_mi + I(dist_ch_mi^2), data = tracts)
summary(m_sq)

-18.5194  -3.0884  -0.0491   2.9256  16.3693

(Intercept)     25.87577    0.69995  36.968  < 2e-16 ***

I(dist_ch_mi^2) -0.12422    0.01908  -6.511 2.39e-10 ***
---

Reading the coefficient: you can’t read either coefficient alone anymore. The effect of X depends on where you are along X. A positive linear term with a negative squared term means Y rises with X and then levels off or turns down. Plot the fitted curve to see it:


Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = dist_ch_mi, y = y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x + I(x^2), se = FALSE, color = "red") +
  theme_minimal()











5C: Categorical variables
Sometimes a number works better as groups, either because the relationship isn’t smooth or because the categories are meaningful. You can make categories from any variable with case_when() or cut(), and then make sure R treats them as a factor.


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    ring = case_when(
      dist_ch_mi < 3 ~ "Core",
      dist_ch_mi < 8 ~ "Inner",
      TRUE           ~ "Outer"
    ),
    ring = factor(ring, levels = c("Core", "Inner", "Outer"))
  )

tracts %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% count(ring)


   ring   n
1  Core 129
2 Inner 179
3 Outer  72


Code

summary(m_cat)



Call:
lm(formula = y ~ ring, data = tracts)

Residuals:

-19.0943  -3.0584   0.0859   3.0684  17.5061 

Coefficients:

(Intercept)  28.7964     0.4533  63.531  < 2e-16 ***
ringInner     4.6945     0.5946   7.896 3.19e-14 ***
ringOuter     4.8470     0.7573   6.400 4.61e-10 ***
---

F-statistic: 36.11 on 2 and 377 DF,  p-value: 4.477e-15


Reading the coefficients: R turns a factor with k categories into k − 1 dummy variables. The category left out is the reference level (here, “Core,” the first level). Each coefficient is the difference from the reference: ringOuter is how much higher or lower predicted Y is in outer tracts compared to core tracts, holding everything else in the model constant. To change the reference, use relevel(ring, ref = "Outer").






NoteCheck your group sizes



If a category has only a handful of tracts, its coefficient is unstable, and in cross-validation some folds may not contain it at all. Aim for at least 20 tracts per category.

Part 7: Reflection (about 300 words)
Answer in prose, drawing on your model log (incorporate our words of the day for bonus points. just kidding):

What helped, and what didn’t? Name the feature that lowered CV RMSE the most and the one that disappointed you most. Offer a reason for each.
Read one coefficient twice. Choose a variable in your final model. Give its β̂ reading and its ŷ reading in one sentence each.
What’s still missing? Look at your final residual map. Name one thing about those places you’d want to measure next, and where you might get the data.
How much of the remaining error might be uncertainty or statistical noise? Use your last plot.

Your answer: Distance to City Hall helped the most. Once I let it curve (distance plus distance squared), CV RMSE dropped from 5.15 to 5.02. The scatterplot made sense of it: commutes get longer as you move away from the center, peak around 8 to 9 miles out, then ease off. A straight line can’t do that.
Job density was the big letdown. I expected it to matter, but it actually made predictions worse (5.20), and logging it only got me back to 5.12. I think that’s because jobs show where people work, while my outcome is how long residents take to get there. It also moves a lot with population density, so it didn’t add much new.
For one coefficient, take the share of adults with a bachelor’s degree. Holding everything else constant, each extra percentage point of college graduates goes with a commute about 0.05 minutes shorter. Two similar tracts that are 10 points apart in college share are predicted to differ by about 0.47 minutes, or about 28 seconds, with the more educated tract having the shorter commute.
My final residual map still has a few stubborn spots: one dark red tract in the north-center, and some dark blue ones in the center-right and south. I’d want to know how good the bus service and highway access are there. SEPTA’s schedule data (GTFS, from 2023 or earlier) could show bus frequency, and OpenStreetMap or Census road files could show highway access.
As for noise, the fog plot shows that tracts with shakier commute estimates tend to be missed by more, around 3 minutes at the low end and 9 at the high end. But plenty of reliable tracts are still missed by a lot, so uncertainty explains part of the error, not most of it.
